facts.claim: "No One Noticed" was written by María Zardoya, Josh Conway and Gianluca Buccellati, and produced by Conway and Buccellati.
It was released on May 3, 2024, as a double single with "If Only", ahead of the album Submarine (May 31, 2024). The label is Atlantic/Nice Life and the length is 3:56.
Zardoya began writing the song in 2020 during the pandemic. She worked on a demo, shelved it for a while, then revisited it as a possible addition to Submarine.

Zardoya said she started writing it when she felt she was competing with technology for attention and affection and felt invisible. She said people forget those in the room because they are on their phones.
In a Genius interview, Zardoya said the label wanted a more up-tempo, radio-friendly song, so this one was put on the back burner. She then leaked it herself about a year later, and fans embraced it.

In a Variety "Behind the Song" session at Electric Lady Studios, the band said the song, first written by Zardoya and Buccellati, helped bring the group back together in 2020 when its future was uncertain. Variety also notes it has an unusual structure.
Zardoya called the song "an anti-pop song". It became the band's first solo Billboard Hot 100 entry and reached the top 10 of the Hot Rock & Alternative Songs chart.

Zardoya and Conway were in a relationship for seven years and ended the romantic part after the first album. Zardoya calls Submarine an album of solitude, exploration and change, and says this song captures what she felt then.

The Marías are a Los Angeles band made up of María Zardoya, Josh Conway, Jesse Perlman and Edward James. They released EPs in 2017 and 2018 and their first album in 2021, and were nominated for the Best New Artist Grammy after Submarine.
Conway is credited on Submarine with bass, guitar, synthesizer, production and engineering across all tracks, so he is the band's main producer and engineer.

research.lineage: The song sits in the Marías' hazy, Latin-flavored electro-lounge, jazz-pop and indie-pop sound, which draws on shoegaze, Latin music and jazz.

draft:
The most telling words in **No One Noticed** sit in parentheses. While the main line murmurs about losing it, a second thought runs underneath like something typed and deleted: "I need a virtual connection." It's the voice of someone who knows exactly what would help and is half-embarrassed to ask. That split between the stated feeling and the muttered one is the whole song.

María Zardoya started writing it in 2020, during the pandemic, when she felt she was competing with technology for attention and affection and felt invisible. She has described how people forget whoever is in the room because they're looking at their phones. The lyric doesn't argue with that. It surrenders to it. The narrator who can't get noticed in person asks to be watched through a screen instead, and the request lands somewhere between a joke and a plea: "be my video obsession." There's also a quieter cut. Only one person ever tried to read this narrator's eyes, and the next line takes it back by wishing that were true.

Then the chorus arrives and won't let go. It repeats four times, and its central move is a contradiction the song never resolves: come to me, comfort me, and then I'm gone. "Hold me, console me, and then I'll leave without a trace" is wanting intimacy and fearing it in the same breath, and repetition turns it from a line into a loop, the way a thought circles at 2 a.m. Zardoya has said the song captures what she felt while making *Submarine*, which she calls an album of solitude, after she and bandmate Josh Conway ended the romantic side of their seven-year relationship. The song never names any of that. It just keeps asking to be held by someone it's already halfway gone from.

The sound keeps its composure while the lyric frays. A drum machine holds a relaxed, mid-tempo pulse with a heavy kick and a dry snare. Bass stays simple, a clean electric guitar picks out arpeggios, and a synth pad lays down a cushion of sustained chords. The vocal is breathy, smooth and unhurried, with no harmonies to keep it company, and the dry, close production leaves it alone in the room. It's the Marías' hazy electro-lounge pop with the lounge light turned way down.

Zardoya called it "an anti-pop song." The label wanted something more up-tempo, so it sat on the shelf until she leaked it herself about a year later. Fans took it in, and it became the band's first solo Billboard Hot 100 entry. The band also says the song helped pull the group back together in 2020, when its future was uncertain. That's a fitting history for a song about feeling unseen.

It sticks because it gives you the exact sound of asking for comfort while already planning your exit, and it doesn't pretend you'll ever choose between the two.
